820.title: Mata Sahib Kaur, mother of the Khalsa
820.hook: at amrit, Sikhs are told Mata Sahib Kaur is their spiritual mother
820.howItsDone: At an amrit ceremony, the new initiates are told that their spiritual father is Guru Gobind Singh, their spiritual mother is Mata Sahib Kaur, and their home is Anandpur Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sundari, sending letters of counsel out of Delhi to a scattered people. Your line was she led. Did you write to anyone? A new week starts today, with a mother. Day eight hundred twenty.

Who are your parents? On most days that's a simple question with a simple answer. But at a Sikh amrit ceremony, once the new initiates have taken the amrit, they are given a new answer, a second family on top of the one they were born into. They are told who their spiritual father is, and who their spiritual mother is, and where their spiritual home is. People come to that moment from every kind of family. Some have lost a mother. Some never knew one. Some have a wonderful one. And all of them, standing together, are handed the same name. Today: Mata Sahib Kaur.
screen: `WHO ARE YOUR PARENTS?` → `A SECOND FAMILY AT AMRIT.` → `ONE MOTHER FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Mata Sahib Kaur was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says she had no children of her own, and that the Guru told her she would be the mother of a much larger family: the Khalsa. And that is how Sikhs remember her. At amrit, the new members of the Khalsa are told: your father is Guru Gobind Singh, your mother is Mata Sahib Kaur, and your home is Anandpur. Think about what that does. A shopkeeper's son and a farmer's daughter, people whose families might never have shared a meal, walk out of the ceremony as brothers and sisters, with the same mother. The family is not made by blood. It's made by the bowl. Two days ago, with Mata Jito, we heard that some tellings say it was Mata Sahib Kaur who added the sweets to the first amrit. Either way, the tellings put a woman's hand in that first bowl. After the Guru's death she lived in Delhi beside Mata Sundari, and tradition says she, too, sent letters of guidance to the sangats. Here is the quiet surprise in her story. A woman with no children of her own is remembered as mother to every member of the Khalsa. Being a mother, in this telling, is not only about giving birth. It's about who you hold, who you claim, who you treat as yours. And every time a new Sikh takes amrit, her name is said again.
screen: `A WIFE OF GURU GOBIND SINGH.` · `NO CHILDREN OF HER OWN.` · `YOUR MOTHER IS MATA SAHIB KAUR.` · `A FAMILY MADE BY THE BOWL.` · then, large: `MOTHER OF THE KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a spiritual mother. Let the breath settle. Think of a woman who cared for you in a way she didn't have to. Not necessarily your mother. A grandmother, an aunt, a teacher, a neighbor, a friend's mom whose kitchen was always open. Someone who claimed you as hers. Hold her in mind for a few breaths and remember one specific thing she did. If she's living, you might tell her later. If she's gone, just say her name quietly and say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Mata Sahib Kaur. A wife of Guru Gobind Singh, named at every amrit as the spiritual mother of the Khalsa. Today's word.
Your line: mother of the khalsa. Today, thank one woman who mothered you without having to, in person, by message, or in your own heart. Day eight hundred twenty.

821.title: Bhai Daya Singh
821.hook: the first to rise at Anandpur, who later, tradition says, carried the Zafarnama
821.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Daya Singh as the first of the Panj Pyare in the Vaisakhi story, and the Zafarnama is read and discussed in Sikh gatherings and schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sahib Kaur, the mother named at every amrit. Your line was mother of the khalsa. Did you thank someone who mothered you? Day eight hundred twenty-one.

Every room has that silence. A teacher asks for a volunteer, a manager asks who'll take the hard job, a friend asks who can help move on Saturday, and nobody moves. Everyone looks at their shoes and waits for someone else. Now make it a hillside at Anandpur, a great crowd, and a Guru with a drawn sword asking for a head. The silence must have been enormous. And then one man stands up. He doesn't know what's in the tent. He doesn't know that four more will follow him. He just rises, first, alone. Today: Bhai Daya Singh.
screen: `NOBODY MOVES.` → `A SWORD, AND A HARD QUESTION.` → `ONE MAN STANDS.`

segments.voice: Before that day he was Daya Ram, and tradition says he came from Lahore. When Guru Gobind Singh called for someone ready to give his head, he was the one who answered first. He walked into the tent. Four others followed, one at a time. And all five walked out again, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved, the first members of the Khalsa. Daya Ram became Daya Singh. Being first is a strange gift. The second person to stand up still has to be brave. But the first one stands into total uncertainty. There's no one ahead of him to show it can be survived. Sikhs remember Bhai Daya Singh for that rising. And they remember that his story didn't end there. He stayed close to the Guru through the hard years that followed. Then, tradition says, the Guru wrote a letter in Persian verse to the emperor Aurangzeb, a letter Sikhs call the Zafarnama. It names wrongs done to the Guru and his Sikhs, and it speaks of God and of broken promises. Someone had to carry that letter across a great distance, toward the emperor in the south. Tradition says that was Bhai Daya Singh. Set the two moments side by side. The first time, he rose from a crowd to face a sword. The second time, he rode toward an emperor's court with a letter that accused that court of breaking its word. Both times, someone had to go first. Both times, it was him. Bhai is a title of respect, brother, and Sikhs use it for those they honor. He's remembered as the brother who stood up before anyone else did.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be first to help. Settle, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind a place where something needs doing and everyone is waiting for someone else. A group chat that needs an answer. A mess in a shared kitchen. A neighbor who needs a hand. A conversation in your family that nobody wants to start. Pick one. Picture yourself being the first to move, not dramatically, just standing up. Notice what makes you hesitate. Then let the breath carry you through it. The bell holds the time.
Daya Singh. The first of the Panj Pyare to rise when the Guru asked for a head, and, tradition says, the one who carried the Zafarnama to the emperor. Today's word.
Your line: first to rise. Today, when a room goes quiet and something needs doing, be the one who moves first, even in a small way. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

822.title: The rest of the five
822.hook: Dharam Singh survived the Guru; Himmat, Mohkam and Sahib Singh fell at Chamkaur
822.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare in Ardas, and at an amrit ceremony five initiated Sikhs serve as the Panj Pyare to prepare and give the amrit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Daya Singh, who stood up first when nobody else would. Your line was first to rise. Were you the first to move on something? Today, the four who came after him. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Team photos have a way of shrinking in memory. Years later, people remember the captain, the one who scored, the one who gave the speech. The rest blur into the back row. The Panj Pyare could easily have gone that way: one famous first volunteer, and then four others who followed. But Sikhs don't let them blur. They say all five names. They tell where each one came from and how each one's life ended. So today, after the man who stood first, the rest of the five.
screen: `THE BACK ROW BLURS.` → `ONE FAMOUS, FOUR FORGOTTEN?` → `SIKHS SAY ALL FIVE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Dharam Singh, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh, Sahib Singh. Tradition says they came from far-flung places and different trades: a farmer, a water-carrier, a washerman, a barber. Men who, in the world around them, would not have eaten at one table. On the day the Khalsa began, each rose after Daya Ram and walked into the tent, one at a time. And after that day, their lives went in two directions. Bhai Dharam Singh lived on. Tradition says he stayed with the Guru through the worst of what came, and was still at his side when the Guru traveled south, near the end of his life. He outlived the Guru. The other three did not. When the Guru's small band was surrounded at Chamkaur, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh and Sahib Singh were among the Sikhs inside the mud walls. Tradition says they went out to fight, and fell there. Three of the five beloved gave their lives in one place. Notice the difference. Some of the five were remembered for how they lived on and kept serving. Some for how they died. The tradition doesn't rank them. It puts them side by side, the way they stood when they came out of the tent. Sikhs keep them together in memory too. The Sikh prayer called Ardas, said at the end of gatherings and daily prayers, remembers the five beloved. And at every amrit ceremony, five Sikhs stand in their place to prepare the amrit. The five keep coming back, as five. Remembering someone by name is a small thing. But it is how the back row gets out of the blur.
screen: `FOUR NAMES AFTER DAYA RAM.` · `DHARAM SINGH LIVED ON.` · `THREE FELL AT CHAMKAUR.` · `REMEMBERED IN ARDAS, STILL FIVE.` · then, large: `THE FIVE, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the five by name. As you settle, say them slowly, one name to each long breath. Daya Singh. Dharam Singh. Himmat Singh. Mohkam Singh. Sahib Singh. Then, if you like, do the same with your own back row: the people in your life who quietly made things possible and never got the credit. A coach's assistant. A night-shift nurse. The friend who drove. One name to each breath. Let each one have a moment of being remembered. The bell holds the time.
Panj Pyare. The five beloved: Daya Singh, Dharam Singh, Himmat Singh, Mohkam Singh and Sahib Singh, the first members of the Khalsa. Today's word.
Your line: the five, remembered. Today, name someone from the back row out loud, to them or to someone else, and say what they did. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

823.title: Bhai Sangat Singh
823.hook: tradition says a Sikh who looked like the Guru wore his plume at Chamkaur so the Guru could slip away
823.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Sangat Singh in remembrances of Chamkaur, especially in December when the martyrdoms of that season are recalled, and the gurdwara at Chamkaur keeps the memory of those who fell there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rest of the five, the Panj Pyare: Dharam Singh who lived on, and three who fell at Chamkaur. Your line was the five, remembered. Whose name from your back row did you say? Today, we stay at Chamkaur one more night. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

Night at Chamkaur. The mud-walled house is ringed by an army that will attack again at first light. Inside, only a handful of Sikhs are left. They have already told the Guru he must go, so the community will not lose him. The Guru has agreed. But an army watches a house like this. If the Guru's tall plume disappears from the wall, they'll know. Someone has to stay behind and be seen. Someone who, in the dark and at a distance, could pass for him. Today: Bhai Sangat Singh.
screen: `NIGHT, AND AN ARMY OUTSIDE.` → `THE GURU MUST GO.` → `SOMEONE MUST BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bhai Sangat Singh looked like Guru Gobind Singh, close enough in look and build that, from below, in poor light, he could be taken for him. So before the Guru left, he gave Sangat Singh his own plume, the kalgi, a jeweled ornament worn on the turban, along with his garments. Sangat Singh put them on and took the Guru's place in the house, where the enemy could see him. Then, in the dark, the Guru slipped out with a few companions. When morning came, the army attacked the house again, believing the Guru was inside. Sangat Singh and the Sikhs with him fought until they fell. Tradition says the enemy at first thought they had killed the Guru himself. Look at what he did, and what it wasn't. It wasn't a trick for its own sake. It was a gift of time. Every hour the soldiers spent watching the plume on the wall was an hour the Guru was further away. Sangat Singh wasn't taking the Guru's honor. He was taking the Guru's danger. Some tellings give part of this story to another Sikh, Bhai Sant Singh, and some speak of the two together. The details shift between tellings, but the shape stays the same: a Sikh who put on what marked the Guru, and stood where the Guru would have stood, so the Guru could live. Sikhs call his name with love. He is remembered not for looking like the Guru, but for what he did with that likeness.
screen: `HE LOOKED LIKE THE GURU.` · `THE KALGI ON HIS TURBAN.` · `A GIFT OF TIME.` · `TAKING THE DANGER, NOT THE HONOR.` · then, large: `HE TOOK HIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cover for someone kindly. This isn't about lying for anyone. It's about stepping into a hard spot so someone else can get through. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone near you who's carrying too much right now. A coworker who's behind. A parent who hasn't had a night off. A friend facing something they dread. Ask quietly: what could I take on, so they could slip away for a while? A shift. A dinner. A phone call they keep putting off. Just find the one thing. The bell holds the time.
Sangat Singh. The Sikh who, tradition says, wore the Guru's plume at Chamkaur and stood in his place, so the Guru could get away. Today's word.
Your line: he took his place. Today, take one weight off someone else, a task, a shift, a hard call, so they can step away for a while. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

824.title: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan
824.hook: two Pathan brothers carried the Guru in disguise as a holy man through enemy lines
824.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan in tellings of the Guru's escape after Chamkaur, and the story is told at Machhiwara, where the memory of the Guru's stay is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Sangat Singh, wearing the Guru's plume so the Guru could slip away from Chamkaur. Your line was he took his place. Did you take a weight off anyone? Today, where the Guru went next. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

A road patrolled by soldiers. Coming down it, a palanquin, a covered seat carried on poles, with a holy man inside dressed in blue. Two Pathan men are carrying it, with a few others walking alongside. The soldiers stop them. Who's this? A holy man, the brothers say, a pir, on his way. They are calm. They are Muslims, and they are telling the soldiers what soldiers would expect to hear. And inside the palanquin sits the man those soldiers are hunting: Guru Gobind Singh. Today: Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan.
screen: `A PALANQUIN ON A WATCHED ROAD.` → `A HOLY MAN IN BLUE.` → `THE GURU INSIDE.`

segments.voice: After Chamkaur, the Guru had made his way through the night, alone for a time, to the forest near Machhiwara. Tradition says that's where a few of his Sikhs found him again, and where help came from an unexpected direction. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan were Pathan brothers, horse dealers, who tradition says had sold horses to the Guru in better days and knew him. Now he was a hunted man, and helping him was dangerous. They helped anyway. Their plan was a disguise. The Guru would be dressed in blue robes, as a Muslim holy man, a pir. Tradition says they called him the Pir of Uch, a holy man from a faraway town. They lifted him in a palanquin and carried him on their shoulders, out through the countryside where soldiers were searching. When they were questioned, they held to their story. Weigh what the brothers were risking. If the soldiers had seen through it, the brothers could have paid with their lives. They weren't Sikhs. They had no duty to the Guru that anyone could have demanded of them. They had known him, they trusted him, and when his life was in danger they put their own on the line. When they parted, tradition says, the Guru gave them a letter, a hukamnama, thanking them, so their service would be remembered. And it is. Sikhs tell this story with deep gratitude, as part of the same thread as Pir Budhu Shah a few days ago and the Nawab of Malerkotla, whom we'll meet soon. Brothers of another faith, carrying the Guru on their shoulders.
screen: `THE FOREST NEAR MACHHIWARA.` · `PATHAN BROTHERS WHO KNEW HIM.` · `THE PIR OF UCH, IN BLUE.` · `A LETTER OF THANKS.` · then, large: `BROTHERS OF ANOTHER FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect someone at a cost. Let your breathing settle. Think of someone who is exposed right now, more than you are. Someone being talked about. Someone new and alone. Someone whose job, or safety, or reputation is on the line. Ask what it would cost you to stand closer to them: some comfort, some standing, some time. Don't decide anything big. Just find one small way to carry part of their weight, the way two brothers once carried a palanquin. The bell holds the time.
Pathan brothers. Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, who, tradition says, carried Guru Gobind Singh past the soldiers, disguised as a holy man. Today's word.
Your line: brothers of another faith. Today, stand with one person who's exposed, even if it costs you a little, and stay calm while you do it. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

825.title: Bhai Moti Ram Mehra
825.hook: tradition says a cook brought warm milk to Mata Gujri and the boys in the cold tower, and later paid with his life
825.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Moti Ram Mehra during the December remembrances of the Sahibzade at Fatehgarh Sahib near Sirhind, where a gurdwara honors him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, carrying the Guru past the soldiers as a holy man in blue. Your line was brothers of another faith. Did you stand near someone exposed? Today, Sirhind, and a gentler kind of courage. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

A clay cup of milk, still warm. That's the whole of it. Not a sword, not a speech, not a rescue. Just a cup of milk, carried at night up to a tower where the winter wind comes straight through. Sikhs tell a heavy story about Sirhind, about Mata Gujri and her two young grandsons held there in the cold, and it's a story we've told gently before. Today we look at it from the side, from the kitchen, through the eyes of one man who couldn't stop what was happening but could still do one warm thing. Today: Bhai Moti Ram Mehra.
screen: `A CUP OF WARM MILK.` → `CARRIED UP AT NIGHT.` → `ONE WARM THING.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Moti Ram Mehra worked in a kitchen at Sirhind, where Mata Gujri and the two younger Sahibzade were held in the cold tower, the Thanda Burj. He was not a soldier. He had no power to open a door. He was a cook. And when he learned who was in that tower, and that they were cold and without proper food, he decided to do the one thing a cook can do. He brought them milk. Tradition says he had to get past the guards to do it, and that he gave them what he had so they would let him through. At night he carried warm milk up to a grandmother and two small boys, and they drank it. It changed nothing about the governor's decision. The boys still faced the court. The story still ends the way Sikhs remember it ending, and we won't retell that today. But for those nights, in that tower, someone brought something warm. Then it was discovered. Tradition says that for this act, Moti Ram Mehra paid with his life, and his family with him. Sikhs remember him with great honor, as a martyr, and a gurdwara near Sirhind keeps his name. Here is what the story gives. Not everyone gets to stop an injustice. Not everyone is the governor, or the army, or the hero at the gate. Most of us are closer to the kitchen. Moti Ram Mehra's story says what a small, warm act can mean when it's done at a cost, for people the world has decided to leave in the cold. That's why Sikhs put a cook's name beside the martyrs.
screen: `A COOK AT SIRHIND.` · `HE COULD NOT OPEN THE DOOR.` · `WARM MILK, CARRIED AT NIGHT.` · `A SMALL ACT, AT A GREAT COST.` · then, large: `MILK IN THE COLD TOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring someone something warm. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think of someone in your life who is in a cold place right now. Not a tower, maybe, but a hard season. Grief. Loneliness. Illness. A long stretch of bad news. You probably can't fix it. Ask a smaller question: what is the warm cup I could bring? Tea. A meal. A blanket. A visit. A message that just says, I'm thinking of you. Let one answer come. The bell holds the time.
Thanda Burj. The cold tower at Sirhind where Bhai Moti Ram Mehra, tradition says, carried warm milk to Mata Gujri and the young Sahibzade. Today's word.
Your line: milk in the cold tower. Today, bring one warm thing to someone in a cold season, and don't wait until you can fix everything. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

826.title: The Nawab of Malerkotla
826.hook: Sher Muhammad Khan protested the execution of the Sahibzade, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since
826.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Nawab of Malerkotla's protest whenever the story of the Sahibzade is told, especially in the December remembrances, and speak of the town of Malerkotla with gratitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Moti Ram Mehra, the cook who carried warm milk up the cold tower. Your line was milk in the cold tower. Did you bring someone something warm? Today, the same town, and a voice raised in the governor's court. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

Sirhind, the governor's court. Two small boys stand before Wazir Khan. The sentence is about to be spoken, and the men around the governor can see where it is going. To object now is to take the wrong side of the man in charge, in public, with your name attached. One of the men in that court is a Muslim nobleman, a guest there, with every reason to keep quiet. He speaks instead. Today: the Nawab of Malerkotla.
screen: `TWO BOYS BEFORE THE GOVERNOR.` → `EVERY REASON TO KEEP QUIET.` → `ONE VOICE OBJECTS.`

segments.voice: His name was Sher Muhammad Khan, the Nawab, the ruler, of a small state called Malerkotla. Tradition says he was present at Sirhind when the governor, Wazir Khan, was deciding what to do with Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, the Guru's younger sons. He was not a friend of the Guru. Tradition even says he had fought against the Guru's forces. And still, when the sentence of death was spoken, he protested. The boys were children, he said, and children must not be punished for what their father had done. Sikhs call his protest the haa da naara, the cry of protest against injustice. Here is the hard part. It didn't work. The governor went ahead. The boys were killed. The Nawab could not save them. So why do Sikhs remember him with such honor? Sikh memory doesn't measure speaking up only by whether it wins. He told the truth in a room that didn't want to hear it, at a cost to himself, for children of another faith. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh heard what the Nawab had done, he blessed him and his town. And Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since. Set him beside yesterday's cook with his cup of milk. Two people at Sirhind, a Muslim noble in the court and a cook in the kitchen, who could not change the sentence and still did not look away. One carried something warm up the stairs. The other said, out loud, in front of the governor, that children must not be punished.
screen: `SHER MUHAMMAD KHAN OF MALERKOTLA.` · `CHILDREN MUST NOT BE PUNISHED.` · `IT DID NOT SAVE THEM.` · `THE GURU BLESSED HIS TOWN.` · then, large: `HE SPOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up for the helpless. Let the breath settle. Think of a room you'll be in soon, a meeting, a group chat, a family table, where someone without much power gets talked about or decided about. A new employee. A kid. Someone who isn't there to defend themselves. Find the sentence you could say. Keep it simple, the way the Nawab's was: that isn't fair, or they're just a child, or let's hear their side. Rehearse it once, quietly, on an out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Malerkotla. The small state whose Nawab, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested in the court at Sirhind that children must not be punished, and whose town Sikhs honor for it. Today's word.

Your line: he spoke up. Today, when someone with less power is being treated unfairly in front of you, say the one simple sentence, even if it doesn't win. Day eight hundred twenty-six, and the end of a week.
